title: Starting a Child Care Center in North Dakota: Licensing, Costs, and Step-by-Step Guide

html:
Introduction

Starting a Child Care Center in North Dakota represents a meaningful opportunity to serve children ages 0-5 while building a compliant, sustainable care business. The state is currently facing a significant child care crisis, with an estimated need for 10,000 additional slots and infant care waitlists stretching from months to over a year. This gap creates a powerful incentive for entrepreneurs dedicated to early childhood education and care. Oversight and funding are administered by the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (ND HHS) Early Childhood Licensing Unit, with reimbursement and program funding coordinated through various state and federal programs, including the Child Care Assistance Program (CCAP).

With a strong market signal of unmet demand and state funding of approximately $65.6 million allocated through 2024 for assistance, quality ratings, and grants, North Dakota offers a high-demand market, particularly for specific niches, but with challenging single-digit margins requiring high enrollment for providers prepared to navigate licensing, staffing, and compliance requirements. Success hinges on a deep understanding of the regulatory landscape and a solid operational strategy.

This guide walks you through every step of launching a Child Care Center in North Dakota, from regulations and licensing to staffing, reimbursement, and inspections. We will cover the critical details you need to know to meet the state’s needs and build a successful, high-quality program.

Table of Contents

  • Understand North Dakota’s Child Care Center Regulations
  • Choose the Type and Size of Your Program
  • Business Structure and Licensing
  • Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan
  • Secure a Suitable Facility or Office
  • Hire and Train Qualified Staff
  • Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans
  • Marketing and Referral Development
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews
  • Frequently Asked Questions

Section 1: Understand North Dakota’s Child Care Center Regulations

North Dakota regulates Child Care Centers through the North Dakota Department of Health and Human services (ND HHS) Early Childhood Licensing Unit. This agency is responsible for the entire licensing scope, which includes setting and enforcing standards for health, safety, staff qualifications, staff-to-child ratios, physical environment, nutrition, and educational programming. The goal is to ensure every licensed facility provides a safe and developmentally appropriate environment for children. Providers serving Medicaid or federally funded populations must also comply with federal frameworks such as the Child Care and Development Block Grant (CCDBG) requirements, USDA rules for the Child and Adult Care Food Program (CACFP), and general health privacy laws like HIPAA.

The regulatory framework emphasizes quality improvement, safety, and developmental appropriateness. This is evident in the state’s Quality Rating and Improvement System (QRIS), known as Bright & Early North Dakota, which offers a pathway for providers to achieve higher standards and receive increased support. Licenses typically require renewal every annually or biennially, contingent upon maintaining compliance and passing routine inspections.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

Before you can begin the licensing process, you must decide on the specific model of care you wish to provide. North Dakota supports multiple Child Care Program Variants, each with different licensing, staffing, and reimbursement requirements. Understanding these distinctions is key to aligning your business with market needs.

  • Child Care Center: A facility-based program providing care for 19 or more children from infancy through school age.
  • Group Child Care: A program, often in a larger home or small commercial space, caring for 8 to 18 children.
  • Family Child Care: A home-based program caring for 7 or fewer children.
  • Specialized Infant/Toddler Care: A center focused exclusively on the high-demand 0-3 age group, requiring lower staff-to-child ratios and specialized environments.
  • Nontraditional Hours Care: Programs offering evening, overnight, or weekend care to support parents with non-standard work schedules. This is a significant area of unmet need.
  • Quality-Rated (QRIS) Program: A center that voluntarily participates in the Bright & Early ND rating system to demonstrate a higher level of quality, often leading to higher reimbursement rates and greater marketability.

Program size typically ranges from small centers with a capacity of 15-30 children to large facilities serving 100 or more. Demand is strongest in rural areas and for providers offering infant/toddler care, nontraditional hours, and high-quality rated services. While urban centers in cities like Fargo or Bismarck may have more competition, the statewide shortage means that even in these areas, differentiated, high-quality programs can thrive.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

Establishing a formal business entity is a foundational step. Providers typically operate as an LLC, S-Corporation, C-Corporation, or a Non-Profit organization. Each structure has different implications for liability, taxation, and governance. We recommend consulting with a legal and financial professional to choose the best fit for your goals.

Once you’ve chosen your structure, you must complete several key administrative tasks:

  • Register your business name and entity with the North Dakota Secretary of State.
  • Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS.
  • Secure required insurance coverage, including general liability, professional liability, and workers’ compensation.
  • Submit a comprehensive licensing application to the ND HHS Early Childhood Licensing Unit.

Licensing timelines in North Dakota generally range from 6 to 12 months. This timeframe is heavily dependent on your readiness, the completeness of your application, passing background checks, and successfully completing the initial facility inspection. Delays are common, so it’s crucial to be thorough and proactive.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A robust business plan is your roadmap to sustainability. It must realistically project both costs and revenues in North Dakota’s unique market. Startup costs in North Dakota typically range from $100,000 to $500,000, covering facility acquisition or leasing, renovations to meet code, purchasing furniture and equipment, licensing fees, and initial operating capital.

Operating expenses are driven primarily by staffing, which represents 50-60% of total costs in a typical child care center. Other major expenses include rent/mortgage, utilities, insurance, food (if participating in CACFP), and educational supplies. Given these high fixed costs, managing your budget is paramount.

Typical reimbursement or revenue ranges are wide, reflecting center size and funding mix. Annual revenue can range from $300,000 to over $2,000,000. Revenue sources include:

  • Private Pay Tuition: The primary source of revenue from families.
  • Child Care Assistance Program (CCAP): State-administered subsidies for eligible low-income families.
  • Child and Adult Care Food Program (CACFP): Tiered federal reimbursement for nutritious meals and snacks served.
  • State and Federal Grants: Various grants may be available for startup, expansion, or quality improvement initiatives.

Due to the high operational costs, profitability is a challenge. Providers operating at a target occupancy of 70% or higher generally achieve single-digit gross margins. This thin margin makes it critical to maintain high enrollment and manage expenses meticulously from day one. A break-even point is typically reached within 12 to 24 months.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

Your physical location is not just a building; it’s a core component of your license and program quality. The ND HHS has specific facility requirements that must be met before a license can be issued. Location selection should consider zoning regulations, accessibility for families, proximity to schools or large employers for referrals, and local workforce availability.

Facility requirements include, but are not limited to:

  • Sufficient Indoor Space: Typically 35 square feet of usable indoor space per child.
  • Secure Outdoor Play Area: A fenced, safe outdoor space with at least 75 square feet per child, equipped with age-appropriate play structures.
  • Health and Safety Features: Adequate lighting, ventilation, child-proofed outlets, accessible handwashing sinks, and lead-free paint.
  • Appropriate Furnishings: Child-sized tables, chairs, and cots/mats for napping.
  • Separate Infant Area: If caring for infants, a dedicated space for sleeping and playing, physically separate from older children.
  • Food Preparation Area: A kitchen that meets health department standards if you plan to prepare meals on-site and participate in CACFP.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

High-quality care is delivered by high-quality staff. North Dakota has specific minimum qualifications and training requirements for all child care employees. Your staffing plan must ensure you meet or exceed these standards at all times.

Required roles typically include:

  • Center Director: Must meet specific educational and experience qualifications. Responsible for overall administration, compliance, and program management.
  • Lead Teacher: Responsible for a specific classroom, curriculum planning, and direct supervision of children and assistant teachers.
  • Assistant Teacher/Aide: Supports the Lead Teacher in supervising children and implementing daily activities.

All staff must undergo comprehensive background checks. Training requirements are extensive and include initial orientation as well as ongoing professional development. Key required trainings include CPR/First Aid certification, Safe Sleep/SUIDS prevention, Mandated Reporter training for child abuse and neglect, and a set number of annual continuing education hours covering topics like child development, curriculum, and behavior guidance.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Your operational rulebook is your set of policies and procedures. North Dakota requires comprehensive written policies that guide every aspect of your center’s operations and ensure you are in compliance with state regulations. These documents are reviewed during your licensing inspection and are critical for day-to-day management.

North Dakota requires written policies covering areas such as:

  • Health and Safety: Illness exclusion, medication administration, handwashing, and sanitation protocols.
  • Emergency Procedures: Plans for fire, tornadoes, medical emergencies, and facility lockdown.
  • Staffing and Supervision: Staff-to-child ratios for all age groups, supervision plans for indoor/outdoor play, and background check procedures.
  • Enrollment and Admissions: Nondiscrimination policies, enrollment forms, and parent orientation.
  • Behavior Guidance: Positive discipline techniques and prohibited actions.
  • Curriculum and Program Activities: A description of your educational philosophy and daily schedule.
  • Nutrition and Food Service: Meal patterns and allergy management plans.

In addition to facility-wide policies, individual care or service plans must be developed, reviewed, and documented for each child, particularly for infants and children with special needs. These plans, created in partnership with parents, outline feeding schedules, nap routines, allergies, and any specific developmental goals.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

With a statewide shortage, your primary marketing challenge isn’t convincing parents they need care, but ensuring they know your center exists and trust your quality. In the professional care industry, referrals are more powerful than traditional advertising. Successful providers focus on building a strong reputation for compliance, responsiveness, and positive child outcomes.

Referrals for child care centers in North Dakota typically come from:

  • Parent Word-of-Mouth: Happy families are your best marketing tool.
  • Local Employer Partnerships: Businesses looking to offer child care benefits or referrals to their employees.
  • State Child Care Resource & Referral Agencies: Organizations like Child Care Aware® of North Dakota connect families with licensed providers.
  • Social Service Agencies and Healthcare Providers: Pediatricians and social workers who work with young families.
  • Online Directories and Social Media: Maintaining a professional online presence where parents are searching, such as local parent groups on Facebook.

Focus your efforts on building relationships within the community. Host an open house, meet with HR managers at large local companies, and ensure your information is up-to-date with state referral agencies.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Receiving your license is the start, not the finish line. Ongoing compliance is essential for keeping your doors open and protecting the children in your care. Oversight includes unannounced inspections from surveyors from the ND HHS Early Childhood Licensing Unit. These inspections are comprehensive and focus on ensuring you are adhering to all regulations in practice, not just on paper.

Inspectors will review records, observe staff-child interactions, and inspect the physical facility. Common deficiencies found during surveys often relate to:

  • Staff-to-child ratios being out of compliance.
  • Incomplete or missing staff background checks and training records.
  • Unsafe equipment or facility hazards (e.g., uncovered outlets, broken toys).
  • Improper documentation of medication administration or incident reports.

To prepare, implement a system of continuous quality improvement. Conduct regular self-audits, maintain meticulous records, and ensure all staff are consistently trained on your policies. Having audit-ready documentation at all times is the best defense against citations.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

Q: How long does it take to open a Child Care Center in North Dakota?

A: The entire process, from initial planning to opening your doors, can take 9 to 18 months. This includes time for business planning, securing funding, finding and preparing a facility, and the formal licensing process, which itself can take 6-12 months.

Q: What licenses are required?

A: You will need a Child Care Center license issued by the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (ND HHS) Early Childhood Licensing Unit. You will also need standard business licenses from your city or county.

Q: What reimbursement is available?

A: Reimbursement is available through several programs. The Child Care Assistance Program (CCAP) provides subsidies for eligible families. The Child and Adult Care Food Program (CACFP) offers tiered reimbursement for serving nutritious meals. Additionally, the state periodically offers grants for quality improvement and expansion.

Conclusion

Starting a Child Care Center in North Dakota is a challenging yet incredibly rewarding venture. The immense need for quality care creates a clear path for impact and business success. This journey requires careful planning, a deep understanding of the regulations set by the ND HHS, and strong operational discipline to manage tight margins. Providers who invest in compliance, high-quality staffing, and strong community relationships are best positioned for long-term success and will play a vital role in supporting North Dakota’s children and families.
